title: A Parasite Gave Tens of Thousands of Americans Diarrhea: Can't Wash It Off, Can't Culture It, Can't Tell Alive from Dead
dek: The oocysts behind tens of thousands of US diarrhea cases resist bleach and rinsing, and only become infectious after one to two weeks outside the body; labs can't culture them or test for viability, so outbreaks are hard to break.
why: This episode turns 'why the outbreak keeps recurring' into a chain of evidence: it starts with tens of thousands of US cases, then shows the lab dead end of being unable to culture or test viability, and ends with what individuals can do about grocery shopping.
who: People working in food safety, fresh produce supply chains, or infectious disease control; also for ordinary listeners who care about 'can I still eat imported salad' and want to understand US outbreak news.
skip: The opening chitchat about syphilis can be skipped; the main thread starts around 7 minutes in with the outbreak overview.

points.h: The US is facing its largest outbreak on record
points.body: Daniel Griffin opens with the numbers: Michigan has surpassed 10,000 cases, North Carolina has another outbreak of about 1,000, and New York City has over 500. He calls it the largest Cyclospora outbreak he has seen and shares his own kitchen clue—the pre-washed, chopped romaine lettuce his family ate came from the suspected Taylor Farms. The numbers aren't the point; the point is that these cases reflect contamination that happened two to three weeks earlier. By the time officials confirm an outbreak, the suspect lettuce is often already off shelves or eaten. This is the starting point for everything in the episode about why it's so hard to control.

points.h: By the time cases appear, contamination is two to three weeks old
points.body: The mechanism is explained clearly around the 11-minute mark: oocysts shed in feces are not yet infectious; they must first sporulate in the environment for 7 to 14 days. After a person ingests infectious oocysts, it takes about another week to become ill. So a single contamination event takes two to three weeks to show up as the cases you see. By then, asking patients 'what did you eat a few days ago' misses the window, and the remaining produce has been distributed and eaten, erasing the physical evidence. This explains why tracing Cyclospora is so hard and why cases are difficult to link to a common food—not because people don't remember, but because the two-week silent period makes the epidemiological question nearly unsolvable.

points.h: Rinsing and bleach can't touch it
points.body: Next comes a set of properties that surprise Vincent: oocysts resist chemical treatments like bleach and routine rinsing, and they are 'sticky,' adhering to leafy surfaces. So bagged 'pre-washed' salads are not guaranteed safe; the problem isn't how long you rinse. A more fundamental lab obstacle is that it currently only infects humans, has no usable animal model, and cannot be cultured in vitro. That means Koch's postulates can't be fully fulfilled, and even testing whether a disinfection method works has no endpoint. PCR positivity only shows nucleic acid, not whether oocysts are alive or dead—something virology has long taught. The more you listen, the more you understand why the US has outbreaks every year yet never finds the source.

points.h: It sporulates only after leaving the gut, unlike Cryptosporidium
points.body: Christina adds the life history and corrects the intuition that oocysts must wait 7–14 days: the close relative Cryptosporidium is already sporulated when shed and can infect the next person immediately. Cyclospora, however, sheds immature oocysts that must sporulate in a warm, moist environment. The life cycle itself resembles Cryptosporidium: sporozoites invade the small intestinal epithelium, multiply asexually inside cells as merozoites, and repeatedly infect new epithelial cells; later, some undergo gametogony and finally form unsporulated oocysts that exit in feces. This 'wait outside the body' design gives it an opportunity to spread through the produce supply chain—the two weeks in transport and storage carry contamination from the farm to thousands of homes.

points.h: An effective drug came before the pathogen was identified
points.body: The history segment tells a counterintuitive discovery order: treatment preceded pathogen confirmation. In the late 1980s, at the CIWEC travel clinic in Kathmandu, Nepal, many expatriates and trekkers had diarrhea lasting weeks. Technicians repeatedly saw small round bodies in smears but didn't know what they were. With no culture or animal model, researchers tried drugs based on coccidian diarrhea and found TMP-SMX (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole/Bactrim) most effective. The pathogen was later described as a new species and named Cyclospora cayetanensis—the species name comes not from Nepal, where it was found, but honors the naming author's alma mater, Peru's Cayetano Heredia University.

points.h: US imported outbreaks could take root locally
points.body: The most concerning part of the latter half is whether the US can shift from 're-imported every year' to endemic transmission. Currently, most US patients have toilets and wash hands; oocysts go down the sewer, and the transmission chain breaks at season's end, waiting for the next summer's imports from endemic areas. But in reality, many low-income people live in multigenerational households, and farm laborers have restroom breaks controlled by employers, so they may relieve themselves in the fields. If this becomes common enough for oocysts to enter soil and irrigation water, and then get 7 to 14 days to sporulate, a domestic transmission cycle could sustain itself without imports. Add that基层 clinics may not do expensive molecular stool tests, so hidden cases are undercounted—the host considers this a real risk.

points.h: Symptoms go beyond diarrhea and can drag on for two months
points.body: The clinical segment turns 'explosive diarrhea' into a concrete picture: watery stools 5 to 15 times a day, large volume, and patients basically live next to the toilet. Daniel says the duration is the biggest surprise—not two or three days, but up to two months in immunocompetent people, and even months in the immunocompromised. Don't treat it just as acute gastroenteritis: reactive arthritis can appear 3 to 6 weeks after infection, and it can progress to Guillain-Barré syndrome. So when the US really sees tens of thousands of cases, the end-of-season public health burden isn't just diarrhea clinics but also delayed neurological and joint complications weeks later.

points.h: Inactivation is only judged by looking for damage under a microscope
points.body: The finale is the paradox of detection and inactivation methods: the paper mentions UVC irradiation might help, but the verification method is still putting oocysts under a microscope to see if they look damaged—Daniel says that doesn't give him much confidence because 'looking damaged' doesn't equal losing infectivity. Molecular tests only look at nucleic acids and don't answer viability; the current genome is even a draft with many gaps, about 44 Mb with high AT content—not that it can't be sequenced, but too few people work on it. The closer to the end, the more the guests admit: much of the knowledge is inferred from related parasites, and the original authors themselves repeatedly say 'speculate.' The real way forward might be to culture oocysts in vitro or in an animal model, or to use other Cyclospora species in the same genus.

terms.def: The episode's subject: a human-specific coccidian parasite that invades small intestinal cells via contaminated produce, causing watery diarrhea.
The resistant form of the parasite shed in feces; resistant to bleach and adheres to produce surfaces.
The process by which immature oocysts develop in the environment for 7–14 days to produce infectious sporozoites.
An autoimmune peripheral nerve disorder that can follow infection; listed as a potential complication of Cyclospora infection.
Inflammatory arthritis appearing 3–6 weeks after intestinal symptoms resolve; a post-infectious complication.
